chief_complaint: 2-week history of fever, jaundice and confusion.
history_of_present_illness: Daily fever started 3 months after leaving a rural area in the highlands of northern Peru, with dark urine, jaundice, confusion, and somnolence noticed in the second week of illness.
exposure_and_epidemiology: Stayed 3 weeks on vacation in a rural area in the highlands of northern Peru (altitude of 2400 m) where he and his wife were bitten at night by tiny mosquitoes, with no personal protection used.
vitals: Blood pressure 90/60 mmHg, pulse 110 bpm and regular, temperature 39.2°C (102.6°F), respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, GCS 14/15.
physical_exam: Patient appears confused and disorientated, without focal neurological findings or meningeal signs, skin and conjunctivae are markedly pale, scleral jaundice, cardiovascular and pulmonary examination are normal, and the liver is slightly enlarged but there is no splenomegaly.
labs_and_diagnostics: Creatinine, electrolytes and alkaline phosphatase are normal; WBC 14.9 x 10^9/L, Neutrophils 13.1 x 10^9/L, Lymphocytes 0.9 x 10^9/L, Band forms 4%, Haemoglobin 6 g/dL, Reticulocytes 8%, Platelets 454 x 10^9/L, LDH 1500 U/L, Total bilirubin 239 µmol/L, Direct bilirubin 103 µmol/L. Coomb's test is negative, CSF results are normal. CT scan of the brain is normal. Abdominal ultrasound reveals hepatomegaly, but no focal lesions. Blood films were negative for malaria but revealed massive red blood cell infestation by pleomorphic cocco-bacillary structures compatible with B. bacilliformis.
differential_diagnosis: Malaria and bartonellosis are the most important differential diagnoses, with rickettsial diseases, leptospirosis, typhoid fever, brucellosis, viral hepatitis, yellow fever, and non-infectious causes of haemolysis as less common considerations.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient progressed to shock, was transferred to the ICU, and required vasopressors. He was started on a combination of intravenous ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone for 10 days. Altered mental status resolved after 3 days of antimicrobial treatment, fever subsided after 5 days, and bacteria disappeared from blood smears by day 4. No further complications were observed during a 3-month follow-up period.
